first.rationale: Three concurrent signals compete for the single experiment slot. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the most tempting reaction to the competitor's move, but its supporting record only documents 'acquisition and revenue lift' for price-sensitive SMBs — not sustained or qualified revenue, which is the actual objective. Matching aggressive entry pricing risks winning low-value, churn-prone accounts and eroding long-term unit economics, so this belief is highly consequential right now yet insufficiently supported for the objective; it needs verification before being acted on or ruled out. In contrast, onboarding/activation decline is addressed by two independently consolidated, convergent memories (memory_31 on signup simplification driving durable first-week activation, memory_86 on shortened onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value). Convergent support across two separate archived experiments makes this the lower-risk, better-evidenced lever to pull this week, and it directly targets both the onboarding-completion and activation declines simultaneously. I'm still spending one verification slot on memory_31 since it underlies the actual action being taken and its original conditions (12 days in) may not reflect current market dynamics under competitive pressure. The second verification goes to memory_73 because ignoring the competitive threat without scrutinizing the belief that promotional pricing is 'effective' would leave a highly consequential, poorly-supported assumption unexamined for future cycles. I am not selecting activation_messaging or enterprise_sales_assist for this cycle: the former has single-source support tied to engagement rather than revenue, and the latter, while plausibly high-quality, isn't the most consequential lever against this quarter's specific declines.

mid.rationale: Verification confirmed the triage was warranted. exp_73 shows the consolidated summary for memory_73 omitted a critical fact: the promotional-pricing cohort suffered -12% 30-day retention and did not survive first renewal, directly contradicting the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. This confirms promotional_pricing must be ruled out despite the competitive pressure — matching the competitor's aggressive entry pricing would likely replicate this pattern of short-term acquisition followed by churn, destroying rather than building qualified revenue. exp_31 confirms memory_31 with real (if modest) numbers: signup +15%, activation +9%, retention roughly flat (-1%), qualified revenue +4%, validated specifically for SMB and not shown to replicate elsewhere. This is a smaller effect than the original consolidated summary implied ('durable lift') but it is net-positive on the actual objective and carries no discovered retention risk, unlike the pricing option. Given this, simplify_onboarding remains the best action: it addresses the onboarding-completion decline directly, complements memory_86's corroborating (still unverified) signal on time-to-value, and has verified, revenue-positive, retention-neutral evidence — the only candidate among the three under pressure with objective-aligned confirmed data. I am scaling as a standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout because the confirmed effect size is modest (+4% qualified revenue) and explicitly scoped to SMB, so generalizing further without a fresh check would repeat the same pattern of over-trusting a consolidated summary beyond its evidenced scope. I flag downstream_value_risk because memory_86 (used to justify pairing onboarding shortening with activation gains) remains unverified and could carry a similar hidden tradeoff to what we just found in memory_73; it should be first in queue for verification next cycle before further scaling.

final2.rationale: Leadership urgency does not change the verified evidence: exp_73 already showed that targeted discounting against price-sensitive SMB churn produces a cohort that does not survive first renewal, i.e., short-term acquisition purchased with long-term qualified-revenue destruction. The doubling of churn conversations this week is consistent with, not contradictory to, that finding — it signals the price-sensitive segment is exactly the fragile, discount-chasing cohort the archive already warned about, and meeting the competitor's deeper cut would likely accelerate losses through the same mechanism, only faster and at greater scale given the deeper cut. Switching to promotional_pricing now would mean overriding a verified, objective-aligned finding under time pressure and reintroducing the exact risk we ruled out three days ago, with no new evidence to justify the reversal. The rest of the candidate set doesn't change either: referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist remain unverified for this cycle's specific SMB pressure, and activation_messaging still rests on single-source, engagement-only support. Continuing simplify_onboarding is the only choice backed by confirmed, retention-neutral, revenue-positive data for the SMB segment under current stress. I am holding scale at standard_experiment rather than escalating to broad_rollout under pressure, since panic-scaling a modest, narrowly-scoped effect (SMB-only, +4% qualified revenue) to answer a competitive shock would itself be an unverified bet. I continue to flag downstream_value_risk on memory_86, which pairs with this action but remains unverified, and recommend it be first in queue when the archive reopens, especially since leadership will likely ask again next week whether the onboarding lever alone is sufficient against sustained competitive pricing pressure.
